intro_cards.title: About these notes
body: Livestock · Forest · Soil water · Farm management
Four units. After each unit there is a **5-question tap quiz** (20 items total). Score updates as you go.

units.title: Forestry and Wildlife
units.intro: Forests and wild animals are one system: trees give habitat, food and cover; wildlife spreads seed. Eritrea once had more closed highland forest (juniper, olive). Much is now woodland, bush or scrub after cutting, burning and overgrazing.

cards.title: 2.1.1 Interrelationships between Forests and Wildlife
body: The interrelationship between forests and wild animals is manifested in a life structure.
The interaction of a community with the non-living environment constitutes an ecosystem.
Every wild animal has a specific habitat in a forest.
Forests provide shelter to wild animals and supply them with all the necessary materials for their survival and development.

cards.title: 2.1.2 Historical Background and Existing Status
body: In Eritrea, forest covers about 1 % of the land area.
With the destruction of forests, wildlife lose their habitats and this leads to their extinction.
Closed to open forest cover still exists in the Semenawi-Bahri and riverine areas.
The mangrove which is marine (littoral) forest is found in the northern and southern Red Sea areas of Eritrea.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Which of the following describes the relationship between the *Ficus sycomorus* (Sagla) tree and its specialized wasp pollinators?

steps.text: **Reasoning**
In a mutualistic relationship, both interacting species benefit.
The *Ficus sycomorus* tree receives pollination services from the specialized wasps, while the wasps utilize the figs as a safe nesting site to lay eggs and feed their larvae.
**Conclusion**
Therefore, the correct answer is **Mutualism**.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: According to historical records, what was the approximate forest cover of Eritrea in the year 1912?

steps.text: **Reasoning**
Historical records show that forest cover in Eritrea was approximately $$30\%$$ in 1912, which subsequently fell to $$11\%$$ in 1952, $$5\%$$ in 1960, and $$1\%$$ in 1997.
**Conclusion**
Thus, the forest cover in 1912 was **$$30\%$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following tree species is a coniferous tree typically found in the dry montane highland forests of Eritrea?
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
*Juniperus procera* (locally known as Tid) is a coniferous (needle-leaf and cone-bearing) evergreen tree species characteristic of highland dry montane forests. *Olea africana* (Wera) is broad-leaved, and *Hyphaene thebaica* is a palm.

**Conclusion**
Therefore, the correct coniferous species is **Juniperus procera**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A forest that has recovered naturally after a major disturbance (such as logging or fire) is classified as a:
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
By ecological definition, primary forests are undisturbed virgin forests. A secondary forest is a forest that has regenerated naturally following human-induced or natural disturbances, differing in composition from the original primary forest.

**Conclusion**
This naturally regenerated forest is a **Secondary forest**.

cards.title: Why forests matter
body: Timber and poles, fuelwood, honey, medicine, catchment protection, shade, tourism, biodiversity.

cards.title: Deforestation costs
body: Erosion, floods then drought, silt in dams, lost species, women walking farther for wood, hotter microclimate.

cards.title: Forests
body: **Classes:** closed forest vs woodland vs plantation vs mangrove on the coast. Conservation: enclosures, enrichment planting, energy-saving stoves, alternative energy, wildlife law and protected areas (wild ass, ibex, remaining elephant range in Gash-Barka).

cards.title: 2.2.1 Classification of Forests
body: Forests are classified based on age, species composition, mode of regeneration, uses or management objectives, growing stock, exploitation, biotic interference, ecology and canopy condition.
Based on age, forests may be even aged (regular) – or uneven aged (irregular) or selection forest.
Likewise, based on species composition, forests can be pure (mainly composed of one species) or mixed (composed of two or more species) intermingled in the same canopy.
Pure plantation forests are called **monoculture**.

cards.title: 2.2.2 Classification of Forests in Eritrea
body: Based on their geographical distribution, forests of Eritrea are classified into four major groups.

Highland forests Highland forests are mainly dry montane forest composed of a mixture of coniferous tree species such as Juniperus procera and broad-leaved species such as Olea africana and their associated species.
Forests at low and medium altitude The forests at low and medium altitudes are essentially composed of dry deciduous forests and tickets.
Mixed woodlands are composed of acacia and associated tree species.

cards.title: 2.2.3 The Role of forests
body: Forests have intangible and tangible roles.
Effective sound barriers: Trees soften urban noise.
Trees, planted in a neighbourhood or around houses muffle noise from freeways and airports.
Trees produce oxygen: In one season, a mature leafy tree produces as much oxygen as 10 people inhale in a year.

cards.title: 2.2.4 Deforestation
body: **Deforestation** is a human-induced process in which an existing forest cover is removed for various reasons.
Natural factors that cause deforestation include volcanic eruptions and hurricanes.
With the introduction of commercial farming, forests gave way to large-scale mechanised agriculture.
Increasing population pressure extended land clearing to steep areas, which were previously unsuitable for cultivation.

cards.title: 2.2.5 Afforestation and Reforestation
body: **Afforestation** is the planting seeds or tree seedlings to create a forest on land which has not recently been forest for example where there had not any trees for the last 20 years, or in an area, which has never been a forest.
Reforestation, on the other hand, is the re-establishment of a forest after the removal of trees for timber.
Eritrea has experienced centuries of deforestation and is now engaged in reforestation programmes to restore these lost forests.
Tree planting initiatives can be undertaken almost anywhere.

cards.title: 2.2.6 Seedling Planting
body: **A nursery** is an area where plant materials are produced under controlled conditions in order to produce strong, healthy, hardy seedlings for planting.
The majority of species planted in reforestation, in Eritrea, are grown from seeds as not many of them are amenable to vegetative propagation.
Seedlings can be raised in containers such as pots or tubes or as bare-root seedlings grown directly at the nursery site or in the field.
Experiences show that, in semi arid conditions, where the amount of rainfall is low and unreliable, survival is improved if containerized seedlings are used for planting.

cards.title: 2.2.7 Time for Planting
body: Planting is carried out soon after the onset of the rainy season, when rain can be confidentially expected during planting or afterwards.
Before transporting to the planting sites, the seedlings should be thoroughly watered.
If seedlings are stored before planting, they should be protected from excessive heat and direct sunlight.
Seedlings raised on black polythene bags can be easily damaged if exposed to the sun.

cards.title: 2.2.8 Enclosures/Closure
body: **Enclosure or closure** means an area that has been put under full or partial protection by restricting human-induced activities such as livestock grazing.
Enclosures are usually located on steep slopes.
Restriction is put in place for a number of years until regrowth of the natural vegetation has occurred.
Enclosures for the rehabilitation of degraded lands have now been widely established throughout Eritrea.

cards.title: 2.2.9 Regeneration Methods
body: Forests may regenerate from seeds, coppice or plantations from seedlings raised in nurseries.
**Regeneration** is the replacement of old individual plants by younger members of the same species.
**Regeneration** refers to the normal growth and development of individual plants from seedlings, to saplings and finally to an adult tree.
Certain processes affect the transition from one life stage to next.

cards.title: 2.2.10 Parkland Agroforestry
body: **Agroforestry** is an integrated approach to forestry which uses the interactive benefits obtained by combining trees and shrubs with crops and/or livestock.
Integration can be achieved either in a spatial mixture or in a temporal sequence.

Agroforestry systems offer increased productivity, greater economic benefits, positive social outcomes and provide a wider spectrum of ecological goods and services, when compared with conventional agricultural and forest production methods.
Agroforestry has the potential to help reduce climate change since trees take up and store carbon at a faster rate than crop plants.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following is a major riverine forest tree species widely valued for its edible fruits and fiber, found along seasonal riverbanks like the Gash and Barka?
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
*Hyphaene thebaica* (locally known as the Doum palm or Arkobkobay) is the dominant riverine forest species along seasonal rivers. It is highly valued for its edible fruits and the strong fiber obtained from its leaves used in local crafts.

**Conclusion**
Therefore, the correct riverine palm is **Hyphaene thebaica**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: One of the following is disadvantage of growing bare root seedlings

options.A: Require regular root pruning in the nursery
options.B: They are less complicated to grow
options.C: The roots are susceptible to air drying during transportation

cards.why: **Bare root seedlings** are removed from the soil without any earth around the roots. Their main disadvantage is that the exposed roots are highly vulnerable to drying out (desiccation) during handling and transport, which can kill the plant.

cards.title: 2.3.1 The Role of Wildlife
body: Stone Age people and hunter-gatherers relied on plant and wildlife for their food.
Early human hunters may have hunted some species to extinction.
Today, hunting, fishing or gathering wildlife is still a significant food source in many parts of the world.
In others, hunting and recreational fishing are sport or recreation and the edible meat is seen as a side benefit.

cards.title: 2.3.2 The Classification of Wildlife
body: Based on their habitat, wildlife can be classified as: • aquatic (freshwater and marine wildlife) • terrestrial wildlife (forest, desert, savannah and mountain wildlife).

cards.title: 2.3.3 Causes of Wildlife Decline
body: Globally, the causes for wildlife decline are diverse, depending on the local environmental and socio-economic conditions.
Habitat destruction and fragmentation The habitat of a given species is its preferred area or territory.
Human settlements decrease the carrying capacity of wildlife.
Consequently, wildlife populations remain confined to islands, littoral or habitat which is in effect island-like for the species concerned.

cards.title: 2.3.4 Human and Wildlife Conflict and Conflict Resolution
body: Areas of conflict between wildlife preservation and crop production are therefore inevitable.
The general framework for organising information about state of the environment – driving forces-pressures-state-impactsresponses (DPSIR) – is used to analyse the problem.
DPSIR looks into causes, effects and possible solutions to the underlying problems.
Driving forces refer to the human activities and socio-economic developments causing the problem.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the primary ecological disadvantage of bare-root seedlings compared to containerized seedlings?

options.A: They are too heavy to transport.
options.B: They are highly susceptible to root drying (desiccation).
options.C: They require expensive imported potting soil.
options.E: They take a longer time to mature in the nursery.

cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Bare-root seedlings are grown directly in nursery soil and pulled up without soil surrounding their roots. Consequently, their exposed roots are highly vulnerable to drying out (desiccation) during lifting, transport, and planting on dry sites.

**Conclusion**
Thus, their main disadvantage is that **they are highly susceptible to root drying**.

cards.answer: They are highly susceptible to root drying (desiccation).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The standard layout spacing recommended for planting most forest tree species under standard reforestation guidelines is:
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Standard forestry guidelines state that the recommended spacing for most tree species is $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$. This layout results in a standard planting density of $$2\,500\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$.

**Conclusion**
Therefore, the standard recommended spacing is **$$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$**.

cards.why: The African Wild Ass is a critically endangered species. The Buri Peninsula in the Northern Red Sea region of Eritrea is a globally recognized habitat and protected area for this animal.

cards.title: 2.4.1 Community Forestry
body: The term “community forestry” is applied in many different ways.
Through their involvement in community forestry, the inhabitants recognize and take advantage of the economic, social and environmental opportunities afforded by their local forest resources.
Participation of the local people is essential in all aspects, including the conservation and sustainable use of natural resources.
The focus, however, of community forest management is on the participation of the local communities in order that they may manage their forests themselves.

cards.title: 2.4.2 Law Enforcement
body: Since then, tree planting on hillsides (afforestation and reforestation), agroforestry and soil and water conservation measures have been implemented.
IUCN has identified six categories, based on protected area management.

The definition and categories are recognized as global standards for defining and recording protected areas and, as such, are increasingly being incorporated into government legislation, and have now been adopted for use in Eritrea.

Strict nature reserves: These are strictly protected areas are set aside in order to protect both biodiversity and geological/ geomorphological features, where human visitation, use and affects are strictly controlled and limited to ensure compliance with conservation values.

cards.title: 2.4.3 Alternative Energy Sources
body: One such reason is that forest degradation has resulted in the reduction of the supply of wood for fuel.
Alternative or renewable energy sources show significant promise of helping to reduce the amount of toxins that are usual byproducts of energy use.
Wind, solar and geothermal energy are all examples of renewable, alternative energy sources.
The rotation of the turbine blades is converted into electrical current by means of an electrical generator.

cards.title: 2.4.4 Establishment of Protected Areas
body: A number of measures have been taken to rehabilitate and restore degraded environments.
Cutting of live trees, hunting or capturing of wildlife and charcoal-making has been prohibited banned.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following describes the core objective of establishing hillside 'enclosures' or 'closures' in soil conservation?

options.A: To clear land for intensive mechanized agriculture.
options.B: To construct concrete check dams across river beds.
options.C: To restrict human and livestock activities to allow natural vegetation recovery.
options.D: To establish commercial monoculture pine plantations.
options.E: To create open channels for rapid water drainage.

cards.why:
**Reasoning**
An enclosure or closure is an area put under protection by restricting human-induced activities and livestock grazing. This passive management strategy allows the natural vegetation to regenerate from the soil seed bank without planting costs.

**Conclusion**
Thus, the objective is **to restrict human and livestock activities to allow natural vegetation recovery**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In parkland agroforestry, why do farmers prune or 'pollard' tree branches?

options.A: To kill the trees and prepare for land clearing.
options.B: To obtain wood for fencing and fuel while reducing light obstruction for annual crops.
options.C: To extract sap for industrial chemical production.
options.D: To increase the height of the water table.
options.E: To prevent birds from nesting in the trees.

cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Pollarding involves cutting back the upper branches of a tree. In agroforestry, this provides the farmer with wood for fuel and fencing, while simultaneously reducing the tree canopy to allow more sunlight to reach the crops growing underneath.

**Conclusion**
Thus, pollarding is done **to obtain wood and reduce light obstruction for crops**.

cards.answer: To obtain wood for fencing and fuel while reducing light obstruction for annual crops.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: All are alternative energy sources for resolving the conflict between humans and wildlife, **except**
cards.why: To resolve conflicts over natural resources, we must move away from wood products (firewood/charcoal) because cutting trees destroys wildlife habitats. Wood is the problem, not the alternative energy solution.

cards.title: 2.5.1 Poverty
body: Maintaining forest in Eritrea requires the development of appropriate management programmes to enhance sustainable utilization of these useful resources.
Factors such as poverty, population growth, the desire to increase per capita income and other pressures put severe strain on forests.
Nowadays, the conversion of forests and woodlands into croplands is one of the serious threats to the forest and wildlife resources.
Overgrazing and fuel-wood collection contribute considerably to the loss of biological diversity.

cards.title: 2.5.2 Beliefs
body: In many traditional societies, wilderness is respected for many reasons, for instance, the wildlife and forests in holy places are conserved.
Modernization does not always favour the conservation and sustainable use of natural resources.
Unfortunately, the notion of “wild” or “natural” is inevitably associated with backwardness and a lack of development.
Modernization implies that the majority tend to change or modify their natural habitat.

cards.title: 2.5.3 Ownership and Responsibility
body: One of the biggest challenges to forestry and wildlife conservation is the lack of appropriate and effective landand tree-tenure systems.
The current land-tenure system is mostly unfavourable and contradictory to forestry and wildlife conservation and use.
Although the Land Law passed in 1994 has officially replaced traditional land-tenure systems, much remains to be done to implement and realize its benefits.
Doubts still exist about the ownership and use of forest and wildlife resources and these lead to the abuse and misuse of these valuable resources.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following endangered wild mammals is primarily protected in the arid plains of the Buri Peninsula?
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
The Buri Peninsula, located on the south-eastern edge of the northern Red Sea region, is the designated protected conservation area for the critically endangered African Wild Ass (*Equus africanus*).

**Conclusion**
Therefore, the protected mammal in Buri is the **African Wild Ass**.

cards.q: Which is a major challenge facing forestry and wildlife in Eritrea?

options.B: Deforestation and loss of habitat caused by fuelwood cutting, overgrazing and land clearing

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Fuelwood demand, grazing and clearing for farms remove trees.

**Step 2:** Loss of forest destroys wildlife habitats.

**Step 3:** Eritrea has low forest cover and limited rainfall, so the other options are false.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

glossary.meaning: Forestry is the art and science of managing forests, tree plantations, and related natural resources.
Deforestation is a human-induced process in which an existing forest cover is removed for various reasons.
Overgrazing is a situation when the livestock population exceeds the carrying capacity of an ecosystem.

Afforestation is the planting seeds or tree seedlings to create a forest on land which has not recently been forest for example where there had not any trees for the last 20 years, or in an area, which has never been a forest.
Regeneration is the replacement of old individual plants by younger members of the same species.
Agroforestry is an integrated approach to forestry which uses the interactive benefits obtained by combining trees and shrubs with crops and/or livestock.
Forest is a large tract of land where trees grow densely forming complex plant and wild animal communities.
Tourism is a guided travel to new places with the aim of exploring new life experiences.
Ecotourism is a conceptual experience, enriching those who research and attempt to understand the environment around them.
State of the environment is a manifestation of the environment created as the result of the environmental pressure.
Wildlife is a source of tourism, ecotourism, materials for research, conservation of natural resources, national heritage and aesthetic value.

questions.q: In a highland forest near Segeneyti, tall canopy trees intercept most of the incoming sunlight, so that small herb species growing on the forest floor receive too little light to grow well. The canopy trees themselves are not affected by the herbs in any way. Which type of species interaction does this describe?

options.A: Commensalism, because one species benefits and the other is unaffected.
options.B: Amensalism, because one species is harmed while the other is unaffected.
options.C: Mutualism, because both species benefit from the interaction.
options.D: Competition, because both species are negatively affected.

why: **Identify the effect on each species.** Record the sign of the effect on both partners. The small forest herbs are harmed (they receive too little light, so they grow poorly), while the tall canopy trees are unaffected by the herbs' presence.

**Write the interaction as signs.** Harmed species = negative ($$ - $$); unaffected species = neutral ($$ 0 $$). The interaction is therefore ($$ 0 $$, $$ - $$) when read from the canopy tree to the herb.

**Match the sign pattern to the interaction type.** From the unit's interaction table, ($$ 0 $$, $$ - $$) is amensalism, exactly matching the unit example of large trees blocking light from reaching small forest herbs. Commensalism is ($$ + $$, $$ 0 $$), mutualism is ($$ + $$, $$ + $$) and competition is ($$ - $$, $$ - $$), so none of the other options fits the observed signs.

**Reject the strongest distractor.** Option A is the classic misconception: it corrects the sign pattern of commensalism. In commensalism one species benefits (for example orchids gaining light by growing on high forest tree branches); here the herbs gain nothing at all, so commensalism cannot be correct.

questions.q: Along a riverbank in the Gash-Barka lowlands, orchids grow on the high branches of a large tree, where they receive the light they need; the tree is neither helped nor harmed by the orchids. Which type of species interaction is this?
questions.answer: Commensalism (+/0): one species (the orchid) benefits and the other (the tree) is unaffected.
why: **State the effect on each species.** The orchids benefit because they gain a raised, well-lit growing position on the tree's branches; the tree is unaffected because the orchids neither help nor harm it.

**Assign signs and match the unit pattern.** Effect signs are ($$ + $$, $$ 0 $$), which the unit's table lists as commensalism, using the very example of orchids growing on high forest tree branches for light.

**Distinguish from mutualism and antagonism.** If the tree also benefited, the interaction would be mutualism ($$ + $$, $$ + $$); if the tree were harmed, it would be antagonism ($$ + $$, $$ - $$). Since the tree is unaffected, only commensalism fits.

questions.q: A woodland herb is heavily shaded by a large overstorey tree and therefore grows poorly, while the tree's growth is unaffected. A student writes that this is competition between the tree and the herb. Is the student correct? Justify your answer using the unit's interaction types.
questions.answer: No. Competition requires both species to be negatively affected ($$ - $$, $$ - $$), but here the tree is unaffected, so the interaction is amensalism ($$ 0 $$, $$ - $$).
why: **State the definition of competition.** In competition both species are negatively affected because they compete for the same limited resource, such as light, water or soil nutrients.

**Test the observed situation against that definition.** The herb is harmed (negative), but the large tree is unaffected (neutral), because the herb takes no resource the tree needs in limiting supply.

**Conclude and correct the classification.** Since the effect pair is ($$ 0 $$, $$ - $$) and not ($$ - $$, $$ - $$), competition is ruled out; the correct label is amensalism (one species harmed, the other unaffected).

questions.q: Historical records show that forest cover in Eritrea was approximately $$30\%$$ of the total land area in 1912, and that this had fallen to $$11\%$$ by 1952. Calculate the average annual decrease in forest cover over that period, in percentage points per year. Then convert this annual loss into square kilometres per year, taking Eritrea's total land area as $$125\,000\text{ km}^2$$.
questions.answer: The average annual decrease was $$0.475\text{ percentage points per year}$$, equivalent to approximately $$593.75\text{ km}^2\text{ (about }594\text{ km}^2\text{) of forest lost per year}$$.
why: **Extract the data from the record.** Forest cover in 1912 = $$30\%$$; forest cover in 1952 = $$11\%$$. Time elapsed = $$1952 - 1912 = 40\text{ years}$$.
**Find the total decline in percentage points.** Decline = $$30\% - 11\% = 19\text{ percentage points}$$.
**Divide by the number of years.** Average annual decrease = $$\dfrac{19\text{ percentage points}}{40\text{ years}} = 0.475\text{ percentage points per year}$$.
**Convert one percentage point into an area.** $$1\%$$ of $$125\,000\text{ km}^2 = \dfrac{125\,000}{100} = 1\,250\text{ km}^2$$.
**Convert the annual rate into square kilometres.** Area lost per year = $$0.475 \times 1\,250\text{ km}^2 = 593.75\text{ km}^2\text{ per year}$$ (approximately $$594\text{ km}^2\text{ per year}$$).

**Interpret the result.** Forest was being lost at an average rate of about $$0.475$$ percentage points per year, roughly $$594\text{ km}^2$$ of forest per year, between 1912 and 1952. The unit attributes such decline to land clearing for agriculture, overgrazing, timber extraction, firewood collection, recurrent droughts and the destructive effects of war.

questions.q: A forest block of $$10\text{ hectares}$$ in the Semenawi-Bahri highlands is surveyed and found to have a tree canopy covering $$15\,000\text{ m}^2$$. Using the unit's classification by canopy density, how should this forest be classified?

options.A: As an open forest, because its canopy coverage is at least $$10\%$$ with a discontinuous canopy.
options.B: As a closed forest, because its canopy coverage exceeds $$20\%$$.
options.C: As a primary forest, because the canopy is undisturbed by human activity.
options.D: As an uneven-aged forest, because canopy cover varies from place to place.

why: **Convert the forest area to square metres.** $$1\text{ hectare} = 10\,000\text{ m}^2$$, so the block covers $$10 \times 10\,000 = 100\,000\text{ m}^2$$.
**Find the percentage canopy coverage.** Canopy coverage $$= \dfrac{15\,000\text{ m}^2}{100\,000\text{ m}^2} \times 100\% = 15\%$$.

**Apply the canopy-density definitions.** A closed forest has canopy coverage greater than $$20\%$$; an open forest has discontinuous canopy coverage of at least $$10\%$$ with a continuous grass layer underneath. Since $$15\%$$ is below $$20\%$$ but above $$10\%$$, the block is an open forest.

**Check the distractors one by one.** B is wrong because $$15\%$$ does not exceed $$20\%$$. C is wrong because primary forest is a classification by level of human interference, not by canopy density. D is wrong because even-aged or uneven-aged is a classification by age, and canopy variation is not the stated criterion. Only A states a criterion and conclusion consistent with the unit, so it is the unique correct option.

questions.q: A restoration team is given a fixed supply of $$5\,000$$ tree seedlings for a dry site on the Buri Peninsula. The unit states that the standard spacing of $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ gives a density of $$2\,500\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$, and that in drier areas the spacing is increased to $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$ to reduce competition for water. (a) Calculate the number of seedlings per hectare at the wider $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$ spacing. (b) Determine how many hectares the $$5\,000$$ seedlings can plant at this dry-site spacing, and state how much more area this covers than the same $$5\,000$$ seedlings would cover at the standard $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ spacing.
questions.answer: (a) $$1\,111\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$ (exactly $$\frac{10\,000}{9}$$) at $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$ spacing. (b) The $$5\,000$$ seedlings can plant $$4.5\text{ hectares}$$ at the dry-site spacing, which is $$2.5\text{ hectares}$$ more than the $$2\text{ hectares}$$ they would plant at the standard $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ spacing.
why: **Establish the area occupied by one seedling.** At $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$ spacing each seedling occupies a square of side $$3\text{ m}$$, so each seedling occupies $$3 \times 3 = 9\text{ m}^2$$.
**Convert one hectare to square metres.** $$1\text{ hectare} = 10\,000\text{ m}^2$$, the unit conversion needed to express the density per hectare.

**Calculate the density at $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$.** (a) Density $$= \dfrac{10\,000\text{ m}^2\text{ per hectare}}{9\text{ m}^2\text{ per seedling}} = 1\,111.1\ldots \approx 1\,111\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$.

**Cross-check the density with the standard spacing.** For comparison, the unit's standard $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ spacing gives $$\dfrac{10\,000}{4} = 2\,500\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$, which matches the unit value and confirms the method. Widening the spacing from $$2\text{ m}$$ to $$3\text{ m}$$ therefore more than halves the number of seedlings needed per hectare.

**Find the area plantable at the dry-site spacing.** (b) Area $$= \dfrac{\text{number of seedlings}}{\text{density}} = \dfrac{5\,000\text{ seedlings}}{1\,111.1\text{ seedlings per hectare}} = 4.5\text{ hectares}$$. Equivalently, $$5\,000 \times 9\text{ m}^2 = 45\,000\text{ m}^2 = 4.5\text{ hectares}$$.
**Find the area the same supply would cover at standard spacing.** At $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$, area $$= \dfrac{5\,000}{2\,500} = 2\text{ hectares}$$.

**Compare the two areas and conclude.** The extra area covered $$= 4.5 - 2 = 2.5\text{ hectares}$$. So $$5\,000$$ seedlings plant $$4.5$$ hectares at the dry-site spacing of $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$, which is $$2.5$$ hectares more than the same supply would plant at the standard $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ spacing. This is why the unit recommends wider spacing in drier areas: each seedling has more soil water available and competition for water is reduced.
